title: Puya (plant)
description: Sole genus of the subfamily Puyoideae
wiki_lead:
Puya is a genus of the botanical family Bromeliaceae. It is the sole genus of the subfamily Puyoideae, and is composed of 226 species. These terrestrial plants are native to the Andes Mountains of South America and southern Central America.  Many of the species are monocarpic, with the parent plant dying after one flower and seed production event.
The species Puya raimondii is notable as the largest species of bromeliad known, reaching 3 m tall in vegetative growth with a flower spike 9–10 m tall. The other species are also large, with the flower spikes mostly reaching 1–4 m tall.
The name Puya was derived from the Indigenous Mapuche word meaning "point".

These terrestrial plants are native to the Andes Mountains of South America and southern Central America.  Many of the species are monocarpic, with the parent plant dying after one flower and seed production event.
The species Puya raimondii is notable as the largest species of bromeliad known, reaching 3 m tall in vegetative growth with a flower spike 9–10 m tall. The other species are also large, with the flower spikes mostly reaching 1–4 m tall.
The name Puya was derived from the Indigenous Mapuche word meaning "point".


Taxonomy
The genus is commonly divided into two subgenera, Puya, containing eight species, and Puyopsis containing the remainder. The subgenera can be distinguished by the presence of a sterile inflorescence at the branch apex in Puya, which are fertile in Puyopsis.

Cultivation and use
Some species of Puya in Chile, locally known as chagual, are used to make salads from the base of its young leaves or stem. A common species is Puya chilensis.
grok_lead: Puya is a genus of the bromeliad family Bromeliaceae, comprising 229 species of primarily terrestrial, perennial rosette-forming herbs native to the Andean region of South America. These plants typically feature long, narrowly triangular leaves with spinose-serrate margins and produce erect inflorescences that can reach several meters in height, often with colorful bracts and bird-pollinated flowers. The genus is the sole member of the subfamily Puyoideae and is divided into two subgenera, Puya and Puyopsis, though recent phylogenetic studies indicate the subgenera are not monophyletic. Distributed from Venezuela through Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and into northern Argentina, Puya species inhabit a range of elevations from sea level to over 4,000 meters in diverse ecosystems, including humid montane forests, dry puna grasslands, and rocky slopes. Many are adapted to high-altitude, arid conditions, with some exhibiting cold hardiness that allows survival in Andean deserts. Ecologically, they play roles in bird pollination and seed dispersal via winged structures, contributing to the biodiversity of Andean sky island habitats. The genus has undergone rapid diversification, linked to the uplift of the Andes and Pleistocene climate changes, resulting in high endemism and narrow distributions for many species. Notable among Puya species is P. raimondii, dubbed the "Queen of the Andes," an endangered semelparous giant that produces inflorescences up to 10â15 meters tall after 40â100 years, bearing thousands of flowers. Other striking examples include P. chilensis and P. berteroniana, valued for their dramatic, spiky architecture and vivid inflorescence colors ranging from blue to orange, which attract hummingbirds and perching birds. Most species are polycarpic, capable of flowering multiple times and producing offsets for clonal reproduction, though some, including P. raimondii, are monocarpic, with the parent rosette dying after flowering. As of 2025, conservation concerns are significant, with many species trending toward extinction due to habitat loss, climate change, and slow maturation rates; ongoing genomic and phylogenetic research continues to aid in understanding their evolutionary history.
